title: NLP
description: Text processing, embeddings, and language tasks — the foundation beneath modern LLMs.
blurb: Text processing, embeddings, and language tasks — the foundation beneath modern LLMs.
careerApplications: Every LLM/AI-agent role builds on these fundamentals; understanding classical NLP also explains why transformers were such a leap forward.

lessons.title: What NLP is
objectives: Describe the range of tasks NLP covers
Explain how NLP scope changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect NLP scope with text vs speech and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: NLP (Natural Language Processing) is the field of making computers work with human language — text or speech — for tasks like classifying sentiment, extracting names/dates from text, translating languages, or answering questions.
examples:
# NLP tasks span a huge range:
# 'is this review positive or negative?' -- sentiment analysis
# 'find every company name in this article' -- named entity recognition
# 'translate this to French' -- machine translation
commonMistakes: Reaching for a full LLM for every text task — a simple TF-IDF + logistic regression classifier is often faster, cheaper, and good enough for straightforward classification tasks.
lessons.careerRelevance: NLP fundamentals are directly assumed knowledge for any LLM, RAG, or AI agent role.

lessons.title: Text cleaning and normalization
objectives: Apply standard text-cleaning steps before further processing
Explain how normalization changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect normalization with casing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Raw text is messy: inconsistent casing, punctuation, extra whitespace, and encoding issues all add noise that makes 'Dog' and 'dog' look like different words to a naive model. Normalization — lowercasing, removing/standardizing punctuation, handling whitespace — makes text consistent before any further processing.

cleaned = text.strip().lower()
cleaned = cleaned.replace("'", "")
# 'the dogs barking!!' -- more consistent, ready for tokenization

lessons.title: Tokenization
objectives: Explain what tokenization does and why it's the first real NLP step
Explain how tokenization changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tokenization with sub-word tokens and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tokenization splits text into units (tokens) a model can process — usually words or sub-word pieces. Modern transformer tokenizers often split into SUB-WORD units (e.g.
examples:
# word-level: 'unhappiness' -> ['unhappiness']  -- rare word, no info to share with similar words
# sub-word: 'unhappiness' -> ['un', 'happi', 'ness']  -- shares pieces with 'happy', 'happiness', 'unfair'
commonMistakes: Assuming 'one token equals one word' when working with modern transformer tokenizers — sub-word tokenization means token counts and word counts are often quite different, which matters.
lessons.careerRelevance: Tokenization behavior directly affects LLM context-window limits and costs, covered further in the Transformers and LLM tracks.

lessons.title: Stemming, lemmatization & bag of words
objectives: Contrast stemming vs lemmatization, and represent text as a bag of words
Explain how stemming changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect stemming with lemmatization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Stemming crudely chops word endings (running -> run, better -> better) using simple rules, fast but sometimes wrong. Lemmatization uses real vocabulary/grammar knowledge to find the correct dictionary form (better -> good), slower but more accurate.
examples:
# stemming (crude, fast): 'running' -> 'run', 'studies' -> 'studi' (sometimes wrong!)
# lemmatization (accurate, slower): 'running' -> 'run', 'better' -> 'good'
# bag of words: 'the cat sat' -> {'the':1, 'cat':1, 'sat':1} -- order is gone
commonMistakes: Assuming bag-of-words captures meaning the way humans do — 'not good' and 'good' can end up looking very similar in a pure bag-of-words representation, losing crucial negation context.
lessons.careerRelevance: These classical techniques are still used in production for simple, high-volume, low-latency text classification where a full model would be overkill.

lessons.title: TF-IDF & word embeddings
objectives: Compute TF-IDF conceptually, and explain what a word embedding captures
Explain how TF-IDF changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect TF-IDF with term frequency and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: TF-IDF weights each word by how often it appears in a document (term frequency) DIVIDED by how common it is across all documents (inverse document frequency) — so common words like 'the' get down-weighted, while distinctive words for a specific document get boosted.
examples:
# TF-IDF: word appears often in THIS doc but rarely elsewhere -> high score
# 'the' -- appears everywhere -> low IDF -> low TF-IDF score, even if frequent
# 'mitochondria' -- rare overall, frequent in this doc -> high TF-IDF score
commonMistakes: Using raw word counts without any IDF weighting for search/relevance ranking — extremely common words dominate the score without actually being informative.
lessons.careerRelevance: TF-IDF is still a strong, cheap baseline for search and document-similarity tasks in real systems.

lessons.title: Text classification & sequence modeling
objectives: Build a mental model of a basic text classifier and why sequence order matters for some tasks
Explain how text classification changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect text classification with sequence awareness and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Text classification (spam/not-spam, topic labeling) can often be solved well with TF-IDF or embeddings feeding a simple classifier — no need for sequence awareness.
examples:
# 'not good' vs 'good, not bad' -- bag of words treats these similarly
# a sequence-aware model can tell these apart because it processes words IN ORDER
commonMistakes: Using a bag-of-words classifier for a task that fundamentally depends on word order (like detecting sarcasm or negation) — check whether your task actually needs sequence awareness before.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing when the simple approach suffices vs when you genuinely need sequence modeling is a practical skill interviewers probe for.

lessons.title: Sentiment analysis & named entity recognition
objectives: Describe two of the most common applied NLP tasks and their evaluation
Explain how sentiment analysis changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect sentiment analysis with named entity recognition and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Sentiment analysis classifies text by emotional tone (positive/negative/neutral) — widely used for reviews, social media monitoring, support-ticket triage.
examples:
# sentiment: 'This product is amazing!' -> positive
# NER: 'Ahmed works at ByteDance in Dubai' ->
#   [Ahmed: PERSON, ByteDance: ORG, Dubai: LOCATION]
commonMistakes: Evaluating NER with simple accuracy instead of entity-level precision/recall — partial or boundary-off entity matches need their own careful scoring, not a naive right/wrong count.
lessons.careerRelevance: Both tasks appear constantly in real production systems: content moderation, customer support routing, and information extraction pipelines.

lessons.title: Evaluation, bias & multilingual issues
objectives: Identify common evaluation pitfalls and bias risks specific to language data
Explain how F1 for NLP tasks changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect F1 for NLP tasks with dialect/language bias and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: NLP evaluation needs the right metric per task (F1 for classification/NER, BLEU/ROUGE for generation/translation) — and needs to be checked across demographic and dialect groups, since language models trained mostly on one dialect or language often underperform badly on others.
examples:
# a documented, common failure mode:
# sentiment models trained mostly on standard/majority-dialect text
# often misclassify text written in other dialects or non-native phrasing
# -- a direct consequence of training data composition
commonMistakes: Assuming strong benchmark performance in one language/dialect generalizes to others — always test explicitly on the actual populations and languages the system will serve.
lessons.careerRelevance: Language bias and multilingual coverage are now explicit, expected topics in NLP/LLM interviews and product reviews.

lessons.title: Practical NLP pipelines & tooling
objectives: Assemble a realistic end-to-end NLP pipeline
Explain how NLP pipeline changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect NLP pipeline with end-to-end and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A real NLP pipeline typically chains: text cleaning, tokenization, feature extraction (TF-IDF or embeddings), a model, and an evaluation step -- each stage's output feeding the next. Standard libraries (like spaCy or scikit-learn's text tools) implement most of these stages reliably, so real projects rarely hand-write tokenizers or stemmers from scratch.
examples:
# typical pipeline:
# raw text -> clean/normalize -> tokenize -> TF-IDF vectorize -> classifier -> evaluate
# each stage is usually a well-tested library call, not custom code
commonMistakes: Hand-writing tokenization, stemming, or vectorization from scratch for a real project when mature, well-tested libraries already handle these reliably.
lessons.careerRelevance: Assembling pipelines from proven components, rather than reinventing each stage, is how real NLP systems get built efficiently.

quiz.q: Tokenization's main job is to:
Lemmatization differs from stemming by:

quiz.q: TF-IDF down-weights words that are:
Bag of words representations discard:
NER is typically evaluated with:
What does NLP scope typically include?
options: understanding and generating human language, in text and/or speech

quiz.q: What is text normalization?
options: standardizing text (casing, whitespace, punctuation) into a consistent form before further processing

quiz.q: What does casing normalization (like lowercasing) help with?
options: treating 'Apple' and 'apple' as the same token, rather than as two different ones
it always changes the text's actual meaning
it's required for tokenization to work at all

quiz.q: What is tokenization?
options: splitting text into smaller units (words or sub-words) for a model to process

quiz.q: What is a sub-word token?
options: a token smaller than a full word, letting a model handle rare or unknown words by breaking them into known pieces

quiz.q: What does vocabulary size refer to?
options: the number of sentences in a dataset
the total number of distinct tokens a model recognizes

quiz.q: What does stemming do?
options: crudely truncates words to an approximate root form, without guaranteeing a real word results

quiz.q: How does lemmatization differ from stemming?
options: lemmatization uses vocabulary/grammar rules to reduce a word to its real dictionary base form, unlike stemming's cruder approach

quiz.q: What is bag of words?
options: a way to represent text that ignores word order, counting word occurrences instead
an ordered sequence representation of tokens

quiz.q: What does 'order-agnostic' mean for a bag-of-words representation?
options: word order changes the representation significantly
the representation is identical regardless of what order the words appeared in the original text
order-agnostic representations can't be used for classification

quiz.q: What does TF-IDF stand for?
What does 'inverse document frequency' in TF-IDF do?
options: increases the weight of common words appearing in every document
reduces the weight of words that appear in many documents, since they're less distinctive
has no effect on word weighting

quiz.q: What are word embeddings?
options: a way to represent words as dense numeric vectors capturing semantic meaning
a way to count word frequency only

quiz.q: What does semantic similarity between word embeddings capture?
options: words with related meanings end up with similar vector representations, even if the exact text differs
semantic similarity has no relation to embeddings

quiz.q: Why does text classification often need to be order-sensitive, unlike bag of words?
options: word order can change meaning entirely (e.g. negation), which a pure bag-of-words representation would miss
bag of words already captures order

quiz.q: What is sentiment analysis?
options: determining the emotional tone (positive, negative, neutral) expressed in text
counting the number of words in a document

quiz.q: What does named entity recognition (NER) identify?
options: specific real-world entities in text, like people, organizations, or locations
the overall sentiment of a document
the language a document is written in

quiz.q: Why is entity-level evaluation different from simple accuracy for NER?
options: NER requires correctly identifying entity boundaries and types, not just an overall label, making evaluation more nuanced

quiz.q: Why might F1 score be preferred over raw accuracy for many NLP tasks?
options: F1 balances precision and recall, which matters more when classes are imbalanced (common in real text data)
F1 is only used for image tasks

quiz.q: What is dialect or language bias in NLP models?
options: a bug affecting all languages equally
a model performing worse on certain dialects or languages, often because they were underrepresented in training data
a feature that improves fairness automatically

quiz.q: Why do low-resource languages pose a particular challenge for NLP?
options: they don't pose any real challenge
there's less available training data and fewer tools for them, making it harder to build accurate models compared to high-resource languages
low-resource languages are always easier to model
resource level doesn't affect model performance

quiz.q: Why do real NLP projects typically use existing libraries rather than writing tokenizers from scratch?
options: libraries don't exist for NLP tasks
mature libraries implement these stages reliably and efficiently, and hand-writing them rarely adds value
hand-written tokenizers are always more accurate
using libraries is considered bad practice

quiz.q: What is the typical first stage in an end-to-end NLP pipeline?
options: cleaning and normalizing the raw text

quiz.q: Why clean and normalize text before tokenizing it?
options: cleaning has no effect on downstream results
inconsistent casing, whitespace, or punctuation can cause the same underlying word to be tokenized inconsistently
cleaning is only relevant for non-English text

quiz.q: What is the classical vs modern NLP distinction generally about?
options: classical NLP uses no computers at all
classical approaches (rules, bag of words, TF-IDF) vs modern approaches built on learned embeddings and large neural language models
there's no meaningful difference between the two
